say.text: A 3-month-old is brought in with bluish lips and tongue. The echo is on its way. No teaching yet: let me see what you already carry.
Which is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Read the stem word by word. Does it name an age group or a setting? Answer exactly the question it asks, not a narrower one.
Transposition is a famous blue-baby lesion, so it springs to mind fast. Before you commit to a superlative, check the stem: does it name an age group at all?
Answer the question as written and choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so slow down on superlatives: look for the qualifier before you commit.

say.text: A resident says: 'Transposition is the blue baby we meet first, so it must be the commonest cyanotic lesion overall.' Which correction is right?

choices.label: Overall, TOF is the commonest cyanotic congenital heart disease
He is right: TGA is the commonest cyanotic lesion overall

say.text: Here is the key. An unqualified stem keys **Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)**: it is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease.
Keep a separate fact apart: TOF most commonly **presents as a cyanotic neonate**. 'Commonest' and 'usually presents as' are two different statements.
Yes. TOF is the **most common cyanotic congenital heart disease**, and its picture varies with how severe the right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) obstruction is.
Keep a separate fact apart: TOF most commonly **presents as a cyanotic neonate**. 'Commonest' and 'usually presents as' are two different statements.
Now a harder one, before I teach anything. Getting it wrong here is useful. A classic exam stem:
Which of these is NOT a component of classic TOF?
Hypertrophy sounds like an add-on, so it is easy to doubt. But think about which ventricle has to pump against the outflow obstruction.
Does that side thicken or not? Try the set from a different angle.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: ask which ventricle faces the load.

say.text: 'Infundibular' sounds like a different site from the valve, so it can look like the odd one out. But a name you rarely hear is not the same as a lesion that is absent.
Think about where the narrowing sits, then try the set from a different angle.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: the unfamiliar word may be the true one.

say.text: 'Overriding' is a vivid word that can sound like a complication rather than a defining feature. Ask whether it is part of the malformation itself.
Try the set from a different angle.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: vivid does not mean optional.

say.text: A student writes the four components of classic TOF on the board. Which list is correct?

choices.label: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, left ventricular hypertrophy
VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, right ventricular hypertrophy
VSD, atrial septal defect, RVOT obstruction, right ventricular hypertrophy

say.text: The four are a **large, anteriorly malaligned VSD**, an **overriding aorta**, **infundibular RVOT obstruction** and **right ventricular hypertrophy**.
ASD and PDA may accompany TOF but are not among the four. PYQs have keyed PDA, ASD and LVH as 'not part of TOF'.
Right. The four are a large, anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy; ASD and PDA may accompany TOF but are not among them.
PYQs have keyed PDA, ASD and LVH as 'not part of TOF'. Current practice lists the four as a VSD, an overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy.
One more stretch before we build. A child has TOF, but the resistance across the RVOT is less than the systemic vascular resistance.
How will the child look?

choices.label: Deeply cyanotic, as every TOF child is
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Blood takes the easier road. Compare the two resistances in the stem and ask which way blood prefers to go.
'Tetralogy means blue' is a strong shortcut, so this is tempting. But it ignores what the stem actually gave you: how the two resistances compare.
Use that comparison and choose again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: let the resistances decide, not the label.

say.text: A 4-year-old with known TOF is playing happily, lips pink at rest. What does that tell you about the right ventricular outflow tract?

choices.label: The obstruction is mild enough that colour stays near normal
The diagnosis must be wrong, since TOF is always deeply blue

say.text: The shortcut has a real source: TOF most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate. But its presentation varies with the severity of RVOT obstruction.
If resistance across the RVOT is less than systemic vascular resistance, the patient is **minimally cyanotic or acyanotic**. Colour follows the resistances, not the name.
Yes. If resistance across the RVOT is less than systemic vascular resistance, the patient is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic, which fits a presentation that varies with RVOT obstruction.
That was your starting map. A memorised list is fragile, so where you hesitated is where we build next: one malaligned septum, and why the four components follow from it.

cards.q: Most common cyanotic congenital heart disease?
The four components of classic TOF?
cards.a: Large anteriorly malaligned VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction, right ventricular hypertrophy (no ASD, PDA or LVH).
